Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 509 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 509 (WMU) covers an 
area of 2,536 km² and is located in north-central 
Alberta, in the Boreal Central Mixedwood and 
Boreal Dry Mixedwood natural subregions. 
F
orests cover most of the landscape (60%), while 
agriculture (20%) is predominantly in the central and 
southern area. The Athabasca River flows 
northeasterly through the middle of WMU 509, with La 
Biche River Wildland in the Northeast corner. 
Approximately 460 km² has a provincial land use 
designation as ‘Key Wildlife Biodiversity Zone’, 
primarily along the Athabasca River. Given their 
localized size and distribution, these zones play a 
disproportionately large role in maintaining overall 
productivity of regional ungulate populations and are 
a source of biodiversity. These zones ensure that 
significant proportions of the breeding population 
survive to the next year (Environment and Sustainable 
Resource Development 2015). 
The objective of the 2025 aerial ungulate survey was 
to assess the status of ungulate populations (moose, 
white-tailed deer, and mule deer if adequate 
observations were obtained) in WMU 509 by estimating 
abundance, density, and the age-sex composition. 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted 
February 8–9, 2025 using distance sampling 
techniques (Alberta Environment and Parks 2016, 
Buckland et al. 2001, Thomas et al. 2010). A total of 67 
north-south transect lines spaced 1.2 km apart were 
flown with one Astar helicopter (Airbus AS350 SD2) for 
a total survey effort of 606 km. Ungulates were classified 
as male or female and by age class (adult or juvenile) 
when possible. Female moose were identified primarily 
by the presence of a vulva patch. White-tailed deer 
were classified as male if antlers were present, and 
female if antlers were absent and accompanied by a 
juvenile. It is assumed that most males have cast 
antlers when late winter aerial surveys occur (Alberta 
Sustainable Resource Development 2010). The 
categories of ungulate activity (bedded, standing, 
moving), and canopy cover (0–33%, 34–66%, and 
>66%) within 10 m of the ungulate, were included as
covariates to improve estimates associated with the
survey. Other wildlife sightings were recorded, including
7 
mule deer and 57 elk.
Results 
Mo
ose 
A total of 79 moose were observed in 56 groups and 
classified as 12 bulls, 48 cows, 17 calves, and 2 
unclassified. The estimated bull:cow:calf ratio was 
25:100:36. The estimated density was 0.336 
moose/km² (90% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.245–
0.460; Coefficient of Variation (CV) = 19.2%) and the 
estimated abundance was 852 moose (90% CI 622–
1,167; CV = 19.2%). Results are summarized in 
Table 1. 
W
hite-tailed deer 
A total of 280 white-tailed deer were observed in 99 
groups and classified as 3 bucks (all with antlers), 11 
does, 12 fawns, and 254 unclassified. The estimated 
buck:doe:fawn ratio was 27:100:109, however, antler 
cast was assumed to be significant and deer tended to 
be in large groups during the survey that made 
individual classifications difficult. The buck ratio is likely 
underestimated, while the fawn and doe ratio is 
underreported as antlerless deer that were not 
accompanied by a fawn(s) were recorded as 
unclassified adults. The estimated density was 1.120 
white-tailed deer/km² (90% CI 0.856–1.466; CV = 
16.3%) and estimated abundance was 2,840 white-
tailed deer (90% CI 2,171–3,717; CV = 16.3%).
